captions.text: Recap of chapter 26: Plan writes up to three steps, before any search happens.
Then code runs every step, and each search can use what came before.
Over 60 runs it tied Split, at 3.5 times the calls.
A plan that looks good isn't evidence. Measure the searches and the cost.
Today's black box: a job that can die halfway through, and carry on.
Let's open it. But first, a job that pays real money.
Six refunds, and a pretend bank: a file with one line for each payment. Once it's in the file, the money's gone.
Run it, and six orders make six lines.
See that os.kill? Right after a payment, the process kills itself. No except, no hooks, nothing.
subprocess.run starts the job as its own process. timeout means it can't hang forever.
Kill it after two payments, then run it again. Predict: what does the second run do?
Exit code minus 9 means killed. The second run says DONE, with exit code 0.
QC-101 and QC-102 were paid twice. messages died with the old process, so it began at the top.
So save the conversation before each model call, and resume from it. Predict: who's paid twice now?
The same two people. Exactly what starting again did.
So read what was saved, before anything restarts.
Two payments have gone, and the save stops at the list of orders.
Why no save between payments? This hook shows what each model reply asked for.
All the payments came in one reply. No model call between them, so no save.
And look at run 1: 77 payments, with no crash at all. A surprise on our first try.
Over 35 runs: every one that finished used one reply, and 2 paid too many.
So save after each tool as well, inside the batch.
Same job, with the full Checkpoint. Predict: will anyone be paid twice?
Better, and still wrong: QC-102 was paid twice.
The bank has two payments. The save has one result. The process died before the save.
Save first instead, and a crash says paid when it isn't. Two systems, and no single step for both.
So stop perfecting your notes. Before paying, ask the real system.
done is yours to write. If it says yes, the tool doesn't run.
One line of wiring. bank.paid is the question it asks.
Six orders, six lines. The model can repeat itself, and the bank's answer decides.
Now crash after payment 5. Predict: what's left to go wrong?
QC-106 got nothing, and the job finished with exit code 0.
The model typed a fake tool_response. No tool ran. It did this in 8 of 9 crashes at that point.
So don't take its word. left asks the bank what's still to do.
ask tells the model what the bank shows. Then it goes round and checks again.
If the tries run out it just returns, so check left yourself.
This is the finished job. The last line asks the bank, not the model.
Same crash, and QC-106 is paid. Six orders, six lines.
It needs a real system to ask. With no outside record, it has nothing to check.
One crash proves little. So 20 crashes for each setup, at payments 2 to 5. Predict the zeros.
Start again, and saving before calls: 70 repeats each. Saving after tools: 24.
once took repeats to 0 here. until_done took unpaid orders to 0: 20 clean of 20.
A few runs never reached their crash, so we count only real crashes.
Read the banks. Most crashes after saving tools left one repeat. Four left an order unpaid.
One left 10 repeats. The restart kept paying until the 180-second limit stopped it.
A runaway reply is rare, and we can't make one on demand. So here's a fake one: 2,000 calls.
max_steps never fires: it counts replies. LoopGuard allows 12. once keeps it to 6.
All of them act after the reply is written, so none saves that time. Hence the time limit.
num_predict caps a reply. 60 is too low on purpose, to see what a cap does.
The reply was cut after two calls, and the job carried on and paid everyone.
So it's a sensible cap, not a proven fix. We've never seen it stop a real runaway.
Your turn. Open exercises.py and complete the five TODOs.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.

captions.text: Saving tells you where you were. Only the real system can say what happened.
The model chose the next step. The truth stayed in the bank.
We tested one job and one 7B model. Measure yours.
